## Exercise 8.1

Zellner's $g$ prior [@Zellner:1986] for linear regression takes the form 
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf{X} &\sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}_0, \frac{n}{\kappa_0}\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\right)\\
p(\sigma^2) &\propto \frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\end{align*}
which gives a prior variance proportional to that of the sampling distribution of the ordinary least squares estimator, which is $$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\{\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}.$$
Note that the prior is conditional on the covariates, which are assumed to be exogeneous.


a) Show that Zellner's $g$ prior gives rise to a conjugate prior and derive the posterior mean and covariance.


:::{.solution}

This follows the same derivation as the Gaussian - inverse gamma model in the chapter on regression models.

The data distribution is 
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{Y} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}, \mathbf{X}, \sigma^2 &\sim \mathsf{Gauss}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n)\\
\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}, \sigma^2 & \sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\left\{ \boldsymbol{\beta}_0, \frac{n}{\kappa_0}\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\right\} \\
p(\sigma^2) &\propto \sigma^{-2}.
\end{align*}

The log posterior 
\begin{align*}
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2) \propto -\frac{n}{2} \log(\sigma^2) -\frac{(\boldsymbol{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top (\boldsymbol{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})}{2\sigma^2} -  \log  - \frac{\kappa_0(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)^\top \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} (\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)}{2n\sigma^2} 
\end{align*}


:::

b) What is the benefit of this relative to an isotropic prior covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf{I}_p$ for $\beta \mid \sigma^2$?

:::{.solution}

The model is now invariant to linear change of units. Indeed, consider the case with a single covariate $\mathbf{x}^{\star}_1 \mapsto 2\mathbf{x}_1.$ Then, the corresponding coefficient $\beta_1$ shrinks, and the posterior would have $\widehat{\beta}_1^{\star} = \widehat{\beta}_1/2$. The $g$-prior directly incorporates the change through the variance term $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}.$

:::

c) Give an interpretation to $\kappa_0$: what happens when $\kappa_0=1$? or $\kappa_0=n$?

:::{.solution}

We can establish that the posterior mean is a weighted average of the maximum likelihood $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},$ the OLS estimator, and the prior mean $\boldsymbol{\beta}_0.$ If $\kappa_0=1,$ then the prior weight for the prior is $1/n,$ corresponding to a phantom observation for a sample of size $n+1.$ By contrast, taking $\kappa_0=n$ gives prior weight $1/2$ regardless of the sample size, which is clearly undesirable as the prior does not vanishes. 

:::
